Metro Transit, a single transit agency serving all of the greater Halifax-Dartmouth metropolitan area, began operations in March 1981.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-TransitHistory-3) The system was created by the Metropolitan Authority, an agency representing the former cities of Halifax and [Dartmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth,_Nova_Scotia "Dartmouth, Nova Scotia") as well as suburban Halifax County,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-10) to consolidate the transit operations of the Halifax Transit Corporation and Dartmouth Transit.

Metro Transit expanded in 1994 with the absorption of the [Dartmouth ferry services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax%E2%80%93Dartmouth_Ferry_Service "Halifax–Dartmouth Ferry Service") formerly operated by the city of Dartmouth. Ownership of the transit service was transferred to the newly created Halifax Regional Municipality when Halifax, Dartmouth, Bedford, and Halifax County were amalgamated in 1996. Since then, the service has been operated directly by the municipal government, and since October 2010 the agency has reported through the Transportation Standing Committee of [Halifax Regional Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax_Regional_Council "Halifax Regional Council"). The municipality announced on July 15, 2014 that it was changing the service's name to Halifax Transit to reflect the city's new brand.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-Halifax_Transit_brand_unveiled-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-12)

### MetroLink

The MetroLink service, a [bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") (BRT) express bus service, was developed in 2003 between the Halifax Regional Municipality, the [Province of Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia "Nova Scotia") and [Transport Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_Canada "Transport Canada")'s Urban Transportation Showcase Program, a five-year program designed to demonstrate and promote urban transportation strategies in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. The program selected cities across the country to showcase a number of different initiatives in reducing greenhouse gases. Halifax Regional Municipality's $13.3-million proposal for a BRT system was chosen, and $4.1 million was given by the [Government of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Canada "Government of Canada") toward this project. The remainder was funded by the Halifax Regional Municipality ($8.06 million), the Nova Scotia Department of Transportation and Public Works ($785,000) and the Nova Scotia Department of Energy ($80,000).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-13) Twenty [low floor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_floor "Low floor") buses were purchased from [New Flyer Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Flyer_Industries "New Flyer Industries") for the MetroLink service. These buses featured air conditioning, high-back reclining seats with footrests, carpeted walls, and ceilings to reduce road noise and vibration, a special livery and logo, and no advertisements both on the inside and outside. One of these buses, #600, was on public display on April 12, 2005, outside of City Hall. The bus was available for media and members of the general public to tour, and increase awareness of the new service.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-14)

The service was launched in phases, with the first phase on August 21, 2005. The first phase saw the construction of a new bus terminal in [Cole Harbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cole_Harbour,_Nova_Scotia "Cole Harbour, Nova Scotia") called Portland Hills Terminal, with a 230-space parking lot, including some spaces reserved for [carpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpool "Carpool") parking. Two routes were created at this time, the 159 Portland Hills Link and 165 Woodside Link.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-15)

The second phase was launched on February 20, 2006. This phase saw the construction of a new bus terminal in [Lower Sackville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Sackville,_Nova_Scotia "Lower Sackville, Nova Scotia") called the Sackville Terminal on Walker Ave, with a 315-space parking lot. One new route was created, the 185 Sackville Link.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-16)

#### Vehicles

In 2005, [Halifax Regional Municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax_Regional_Municipality "Halifax Regional Municipality") purchased twenty new buses from [New Flyer Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Flyer_Industries "New Flyer Industries") of [Winnipeg, Manitoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnipeg,_Manitoba "Winnipeg, Manitoba"). It was assumed at the time that HRM would purchase New Flyer's D40i Invero model, which New Flyer was marketing towards [BRT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") services, however HRM resisted and ordered 20 model D40LF instead, and were given fleet numbers 600 - 619. The D40LF was the current bus of choice at the time for Halifax Transit's regular fleet, so they opted to keep the status quo.

These twenty buses featured a new [livery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livery "Livery") on the outside, air conditioning on the inside (a first for Halifax Transit), bike racks, carpeting on the walls and ceiling to reduce road noise and vibrations, and larger plush high-back reclining chairs with arm and leg rests and custom designed fabric design. Also differentiating these buses from the rest of the Halifax Transit fleet are onboard transmitters for the [3M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3M "3M")[Opticom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opticom_System "Opticom System") system. Opticom is the system in place in HRM used by fire services and MetroLink, to allow emergency and transit vehicles to hold green lights and prevent them from turning red until the vehicle has passed through the intersection. The system was also used to trigger transit priority signals at certain intersections, allowing MetroLink buses to move into the intersection using special bus-only lanes before the rest of the vehicles can proceed. This allowed MetroLink buses at a red light to "jump" ahead of waiting cars.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-17)

#### Fares

Effective September 1, 2024,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-18) the MetroLink service had its own fare structure, separate from the rest of the Halifax Transit system. Cash fares cost an extra fifty cents over and above the regular fares. MetroLink had its own monthly bus pass, the MetroLink Pass, which could have been used on any Halifax Transit service. Passengers would have been able to use regular transit tickets or monthly bus passes (MetroPass), but they must deposit an additional fifty cents into the farebox.

#### Bus stops

Part of Halifax Regional Municipality's plans for distinguishing the MetroLink service from the rest of the Halifax Transit system involved creating special bus stop signs, bus shelters and info posts at MetroLink bus stops. The new bus stop signs featured the same colours and design as the livery on the buses, the new shelters featured the gold and blue MetroLink "swirl" along the back wall, and the new info posts, which displayed maps and schedule information for the three former MetroLink routes, they were also done in the same gold and blue swirl, with the stop name vertically oriented along the side.

#### Traffic changes

A number of changes were made to streets and intersections along the routes to help the MetroLink buses get ahead of the rest of traffic.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-19) The following changes were introduced:

*   Bus-only lanes and traffic priority signals along Portland Street in [Dartmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth,_Nova_Scotia "Dartmouth, Nova Scotia") for the route 159 and 165. The lanes and signals are located at the intersection of Portland Street and Woodlawn Road. The bus-only lanes allowed the MetroLink buses to bypass traffic waiting at a red light. Just before the light turns green, a special transit priority signal (a white vertical bar above the red stop light) comes on, allowing the bus to enter the intersection ahead of waiting vehicles.
*   Bus-only lanes and traffic priority signals along Windmill Road in the [Burnside Industrial Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnside_Industrial_Park "Burnside Industrial Park") for the route 185. The lanes and signals are located at the intersections of Windmill Road, Wright Ave and Akerley Blvd. They work in the same manner as described above.

#### Former planned development

Phase three of the MetroLink service was expected to take place within the next five years of the first three lines. This phase would have seen new terminals and MetroLink routes in other busy corridors such as [Clayton Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Park,_Nova_Scotia "Clayton Park, Nova Scotia") and [Spryfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spryfield,_Nova_Scotia "Spryfield, Nova Scotia").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-20)

Plans existed to introduce a new route to service the Cobequid Terminal, also in [Lower Sackville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Sackville,_Nova_Scotia "Lower Sackville, Nova Scotia") shortly after the 185 Sackville Link came into service. Destination signs on board the buses were even programmed with a route 184 Cobequid, and early maps of the MetroLink service showed a route 184 between Cobequid Terminal and [downtown Halifax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Halifax "Downtown Halifax"), however this plan seems to have been abandoned.

#### Impacts

*   The route 185 Sackville Line improved transit connections to downtown Halifax from Lower Sackville, since standard bus service on routes 87 & 1 takes 43 minutes in optimal conditions, and bus service on the route 80 (which travels via [Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedford,_Nova_Scotia "Bedford, Nova Scotia")) takes 1 hour 10 minutes.
*   Both routes 159 Portland Hills Link and 185 Sackville Link saw unprecedented ridership in the first few months of service. Initial rush hour schedules saw both routes running on 15-minute frequencies, however within months this was changed to 10-minutes. Also, both Portland Hills Terminal and the Sackville Terminal underwent expansions to their parking lots, bringing the combined capacity of both lots to 545 cars. Still, both parking lots were frequently full, with people parking on the driveways to the lots.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-21)

### Fuel leak

In 2014, a massive fuel leak spilling close to 200,000 litres of fuel at Halifax Transit's Burnside bus depot went undetected for almost four months.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-22) In addition to the cost of lost fuel, cleanup from local environmental damage and groundwater contamination as far as 1 km away cost Halifax Regional Municipality approximately $2.5 million.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-23) Before the discovery of the leak, Halifax Transit initially claimed that the excess fuel consumption was caused by higher usage during winter.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-24)

The municipal auditor general investigated the incident and recommended that Halifax Transit improve monitoring of fuel usage and inventory and improve training of employees involved in fuel handling.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-agfuel-25)

### System redesign

In January 2014, Halifax Regional Council approved a study to look at a major re-design of the city's transit system.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-26) The "Moving Forward Together Plan" (MFTP) was adopted in-principle by the council in April 2016. Proposed amendments to the plan were defeated in November 2016, with the exception of a change to the route of the Porters Lake MetroX and a short reprieve to attempt to increase ridership to save the #15 bus to York Redoubt.

The Moving Forward Together Plan is Halifax Transit's five-year improvement plan that outlines planned changes to the transit network from late 2016 to 2020. The plan aims to increase the proportion of resources dedicated to high-ridership routes, simplify the system and make it more understandable, improve service quality and reliability, and give priority to transit in the transportation network.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-movingforwardpage-27) The plan created a new classification system for bus routes, designating them as corridor, local, express, regional express, or rural routes. Corridor routes form the backbone of the revamped bus system, providing frequent service connecting transit terminals.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-MFTPplan-28)

Some critics called the plan inadequate, outlining various criticisms including inefficient and redundant route design, missing data and analysis, a long implementation period causing nuisance to riders, and a lack of network connectivity. In addition, critics characterised the "Moving Forward Together Plan" as disregarding the key principles that Halifax Transit identified through years of public engagement and consultation.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-29) Business groups have also noted both the current lack of service, and lack of proposed future service, along key corridors of the region.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-30)

The changes proposed under the Moving Forward Together Plan were implemented in stages each year, with the first round of changes taking place during the 2017/18 fiscal year. The final changes were delayed due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Nova_Scotia "COVID-19 pandemic in Nova Scotia") and chronic staffing shortages, but were ultimately completed during the 2024/25 fiscal year.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-31)

### Bus services

There are 369 conventional buses in the fleet,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-202122businessplan-4) all of which are low floor and wheelchair accessible.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-metro2017-32)

Halifax Transit operates 63 conventional bus routes within the Urban Transit Service Boundary, broadly similar to the [metropolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area") region of [Halifax Regional Municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax_Regional_Municipality,_Nova_Scotia "Halifax Regional Municipality, Nova Scotia") ([Halifax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax,_Nova_Scotia_(former_city) "Halifax, Nova Scotia (former city)"), [Dartmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth,_Nova_Scotia "Dartmouth, Nova Scotia"), [Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedford,_Nova_Scotia "Bedford, Nova Scotia") and [Sackville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Sackville,_Nova_Scotia "Lower Sackville, Nova Scotia")), including the areas of [Eastern Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Passage,_Nova_Scotia "Eastern Passage, Nova Scotia"), [North Preston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Preston,_Nova_Scotia "North Preston, Nova Scotia")/[Cherry Brook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherry_Brook,_Nova_Scotia "Cherry Brook, Nova Scotia") and [Herring Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herring_Cove,_Nova_Scotia "Herring Cove, Nova Scotia"). Routes are numbered according to the region or type of service provided. The agency also operates three regional express routes and three rural routes.

The bus fleet is stored and maintained at two depots, namely the Burnside Transit Centre and the Ragged Lake Transit Centre.

#### Corridor routes

_Corridor routes_ are higher-ridership routes that provide frequent service for most of the day. They serve major destinations and transit terminals.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-MFTPplan-28) Following the round of service adjustments implemented in November 2021, there are ten corridor routes, numbered 1-10.

Corridor routes, considered the backbone of the bus system, operate at headways of 5–15 minutes during peak hours.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-MFTPplan-28)

#### Local routes

_Local routes_ provide connect neighbourhoods to corridor routes (at transit terminals).[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-MFTPplan-28) Local routes operate all day, except for four routes that operate at peak hours only: 26, 50, 57, and 93 (as well as parts of route 51).

#### Express routes

_Express routes_ provide limited-stop services to major destinations (e.g. downtown Halifax) at peak hours. Express bus stops are designated with a red route decal.

Express routes are sometimes paired with a local route, providing service along the local route before continuing along the express portion of the journey. For example, route 182 First Lake Express is an extended version of route 82 First Lake.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-MFTPplan-28)

This service type consolidated the former [MetroLink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MetroLink_(Halifax) "MetroLink (Halifax)") and "Urban Express" services.

#### Regional Express routes

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/MetroX_bus_at_Halifax_airport_2018.jpg/250px-MetroX_bus_at_Halifax_airport_2018.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MetroX_bus_at_Halifax_airport_2018.jpg)

A regional express bus (route 320) serving Halifax Stanfield International Airport

_Regional Express routes_ connect outlying areas to the regional centre. A higher fare is charged for these routes.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-MFTPplan-28)

Also branded as [MetroX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MetroX_(Halifax) "MetroX (Halifax)"), there are three Regional Express routes. These started operating in August 2009 and connect Tantallon, the Airport, and Porters Lake, respectively, to [Scotia Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotia_Square "Scotia Square") in downtown Halifax. The routes are handicap accessible and have facilities for bicycle carriage.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-33)

Among the three Regional Express routes, only route 320 (serving the airport) provides service on the weekend.

#### Rural routes

_Rural routes_ provide service to areas outside the Urban Transit Service Boundary which had transit service before the boundary was adopted.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-MFTPplan-28) There are three such routes, which connect rural areas to the nearest bus terminal.

### Ferry services

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/2022-08-15_01_Halifax_Transit_ferry%2C_VINCENT_COLEMAN_-_IMO_9850317_-_Canada.jpg/250px-2022-08-15_01_Halifax_Transit_ferry%2C_VINCENT_COLEMAN_-_IMO_9850317_-_Canada.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2022-08-15_01_Halifax_Transit_ferry,_VINCENT_COLEMAN_-_IMO_9850317_-_Canada.jpg)

Halifax Transit ferry, _Vincent Coleman_, arriving from Alderney Landing

Main article: [Halifax-Dartmouth Ferry Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax-Dartmouth_Ferry_Service "Halifax-Dartmouth Ferry Service")

Halifax Transit also provides two passenger ferry routes, one connecting [downtown Halifax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Halifax "Downtown Halifax") with [Alderney Landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alderney_Landing "Alderney Landing") in Dartmouth, and the other connecting with [Woodside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodside,_Nova_Scotia "Woodside, Nova Scotia"). Each route is serviced by a pair of vessels. The ferry services are integrated with the bus services; the fares are identical, and transfers are accepted between the two systems. The harbour ferries boarded approximately 1.7 million passengers in the 2024/25 fiscal year.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-202425report-2) Each ferry carries up to 398 passengers. All routes are handicap accessible and have provision to carry bicycles.

The agency operates a fleet of five ferries built in the 2010s by [A. F. Theriault Shipyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._F._Theriault_Shipyard "A. F. Theriault Shipyard"). As of 2023, a third ferry route – connecting downtown Halifax and Bedford – is in planning.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-34)

### Access-A-Bus

Halifax Transit also provides Access-A-Bus, a dial-a-ride paratransit service for people who cannot use the conventional transit service due to physical or cognitive disability.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-accessabus-35) This was created in 1981, the same year Metro Transit was formed.

In the 2024/25 financial year, the Access-A-Bus service had approximately 171,000 boardings.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-202425report-2)

### Fares and passes

Halifax Transit has four main fare categories: Adult (18 years & up), Senior (65+ years), Child (13 – 17 years), and Student (for full-time students with valid student photo ID card). Anyone with a ticket, pass or transfer for the regular service can pay the difference in cash fare to use the more expensive Regional Express (MetroX) service. Monthly passes allow for unlimited use of ferries and buses, and are sold through various channels including municipal service centres, drug stores, some supermarkets, and the convenience store at the Bridge Terminal.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-passes-36)

Digital tickets and passes can be purchased using HFXGO, the agency's free mobile fare payment app. Launched on November 2, 2023, the app is available for Android and iOS devices.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-37) Initially, digital tickets or passes had to be shown to the bus driver or ferry terminal attendant upon boarding.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-38) Fare validation machines have since been installed at ferry terminals and on buses.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-39)

A Canadian National Institute for the Blind (CNIB) identification card can be used to obtain free travel on Halifax Transit's buses and ferries. A university student bus pass (called U-pass) is available to students of [Saint Mary's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Mary's_University_(Halifax) "Saint Mary's University (Halifax)"), [Mount Saint Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Saint_Vincent_University "Mount Saint Vincent University"), [King's College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_King's_College "University of King's College"), [Dalhousie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalhousie_University "Dalhousie University"), [Nova Scotia Community College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia_Community_College "Nova Scotia Community College") (Halifax campuses) and [Nova Scotia College of Art and Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia_College_of_Art_and_Design_University "Nova Scotia College of Art and Design University"). The cost is included in tuition fees. Halifax Transit offers a low-income bus pass sold for 50 per cent of the regular price to eligible applicants.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-lowincomeprogram-40)

In 2021, Halifax Transit launched a pilot program to provide high school students with free transit passes. The program aims to provide youth with convenient transportation and encourage the use of public transit. The program is currently being piloted at all schools in the [HRCE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax_Regional_Centre_for_Education "Halifax Regional Centre for Education"), and CSAP schools in the Halifax Regional Municipality, as well as for home-schooled students in the region, namely [Dartmouth High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth_High_School_(Nova_Scotia) "Dartmouth High School (Nova Scotia)"), [École Mosaïque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_Mosa%C3%AFque?action=edit&redlink=1 "École Mosaïque (page does not exist)"), [École du Sommet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_du_Sommet "École du Sommet"), and [Prince Andrew High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Andrew_High_School "Prince Andrew High School").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-41) In November 2022, council voted to expand the program to four Dartmouth junior high schools.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-signalnov2022-42)

Transfers are issued upon request on all Halifax Transit buses and ferries. A transfer allows the user to transfer between multiple conventional route buses and ferries travelling in any direction without having to pay an additional fare. A transfer also allows users to transfer to [MetroX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MetroX_(Halifax) "MetroX (Halifax)") buses at a reduced fare. Transfers are valid for 90 minutes after the last scheduled stop on the current run of the route where it was issued. Holders of a valid XPass (the monthly pass for the MetroX) do not require transfers.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-43)

### Schedules and route information

Route information can be accessed through the Halifax Transit Departures number, (902) 480-8000. Individual route schedules are available on Halifax Transit's website. Most terminals have screens that display anticipated arrival times of buses that service the terminal.

### Departures

In early 2016, Halifax Transit released their next-generation AVL-based system called Departures. The system was first launched on May 15, 2016, with the introduction of the Departures Line, and as of July 2016 the rollout of the updated Departures Board that replaces the older GoTime departure displays found at terminals across the system. The Departures Board works similar to the previous GoTime-based departures display, with the exception that instead of showing the next two bus arrival times, will display the bay number and the next bus departure time, either showing the next hour and minute or the number of minutes before the bus departs, or "delayed" if the bus is behind by a certain number of minutes. It will also only show buses set to arrive in the next while, versus the older display which would show "(not scheduled)" for any route not running at that point in time.

The Departures Line works similarly to the previous GoTime IVR (Interactive Voice Response) system. Instead of dialing "(902) 480-" plus the four-digit number found on bus stop signage, one dials (902) 480-8000 and following the voice responses, one would input the bus stop number to access route departure times. The system gives the estimated departure time if available, scheduled times if the bus is not reporting real-time data or is delayed by a number of minutes, adjusted time to depart when schedule adjustments are made, and will announce when a bus is arriving within the minute.

### Accessibility

On December 16, 2016 Halifax Transit began piloting an automated stop announcement system on several bus routes, providing both auditory and visual notice of approaching bus stops, as well as announcing the route of each bus on arrival at a bus stop.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-44) By January 30, 2017, all conventional buses provided the automated stop announcement.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-45) As of June 8, 2017, all conventional buses in the Halifax Transit fleet were low floor and accessible to wheelchairs.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-metro2017-32)

Although Halifax Transit's vehicle fleet is considered accessible, many of the bus stops are not. At some stops, the lack of an appropriate landing area prevents the deployment of a bus [wheelchair ramp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheelchair_ramp "Wheelchair ramp"). Other stops lack sidewalk connections. Halifax Transit is upgrading bus stops and aims to make all stops accessible by 2030.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-46)

### Route number structure

As mentioned above, the Moving Forward Together Plan created a new classification system for bus routes, which is reflected in a new route numbering system:

*   Corridor routes (numbered 1-19)
*   Local routes (numbered 20-99)
*   Express routes (numbered 100-199)
*   Regional Express routes (numbered 300-399)
*   Rural routes (numbered 400-499)

## Rapid Transit Network

In May 2020, Halifax Transit presented a plan to regional council to implement a new Rapid Transit Strategy. The strategy proposes the creation of a new Rapid Transit Network comprising four new bus rapid transit (BRT) lines and three new ferry routes. The estimated capital cost is around C$300–325 million, while operational costs are estimated at $15–22 million.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-47) Halifax Regional Council unanimously endorsed the plan on May 26, 2020.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-endorsecbc-48)

As of 2021, Halifax is seeking funding for the project from other levels of government.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-abmmarch2021-49) Funding for the planning and design of one of the proposed ferry routes, the Halifax-Mill Cove (Bedford) service, was announced in June 2021. Halifax Transit originally planned to launch the service in 2024.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-50)[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]

## In popular culture

*   The characters of Phillip and Phillmore the ferry twins from the children's TV show _[Theodore Tugboat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore\_Tugboat "Theodore Tugboat")_ are modelled after the Halifax-Dartmouth ferries.

**Halifax Transit** is a Canadian [public transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_transport "Public transport") service operating buses and ferries in [Halifax, Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax,_Nova_Scotia "Halifax, Nova Scotia"). Founded as **Metro Transit** in March 1981, the agency runs two [ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax%E2%80%93Dartmouth_Ferry_Service "Halifax–Dartmouth Ferry Service") routes, 63 conventional bus routes (including corridor, local, and express services), three regional express routes (called MetroX), and three rural routes. Halifax Transit also operates Access-a-Bus, a door-to-door paratransit service for senior and disabled citizens.

Total ridership in the 2024/25 fiscal year was about 32.3 million, with the system carrying an average of 103,165 on weekdays.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-202425report-2) According to the [2016 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Canadian_census "2016 Canadian census"), Halifax had the seventh-highest proportion of workers taking transit to work among Canadian cities.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-2016census-5)

## History

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Manager_James_Adams_and_most_of_conductors%2C_drivers%2C_etc.%2C_with_two_open_%28summer%29_horse_cars%2C_Halifax_Street_Railway_Co.%2C_Halifax%2C_N.S.%2C_ca._1894.jpg/250px-Manager_James_Adams_and_most_of_conductors%2C_drivers%2C_etc.%2C_with_two_open_%28summer%29_horse_cars%2C_Halifax_Street_Railway_Co.%2C_Halifax%2C_N.S.%2C_ca._1894.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manager_James_Adams_and_most_of_conductors,_drivers,_etc.,_with_two_open_(summer)_horse_cars,_Halifax_Street_Railway_Co.,_Halifax,_N.S.,_ca._1894.jpg)

Two open (summer) horse cars of the Halifax Street Railway Co, 1894

### Preceding services

Halifax was among the first Canadian cities to be served by an integrated public transportation system, pre-dated only by [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"), [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal") and [Quebec City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_City "Quebec City").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-6)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

The city's first transit service came with the establishment of the [Dartmouth ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax-Dartmouth_Ferry_Service "Halifax-Dartmouth Ferry Service") service, first chartered in 1752. In 1816, the sail-powered ferry was replaced by a horse-powered boat, and in 1830 by a steam ferry. While private [horse-drawn omnibus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse-drawn_omnibus "Horse-drawn omnibus") services are known to have begun in the city at least as early as 1854, the roots of Halifax Transit date back to June 11, 1866.

The [Halifax City Railroad Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia_Light_and_Power "Nova Scotia Light and Power") (HCR) began operations with five horse-drawn trams on rails that stretched from the corner of Barrington Street and Inglis Street in the south end to the city’s first railway station, near the corner of Duffus Street and Campbell Road (now Barrington Street), in the north end.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-7)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Tram_Plow%2C_Halifax.jpg/250px-Tram_Plow%2C_Halifax.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tram_Plow,_Halifax.jpg)

Tram with plow attachment, 1930s

Notwithstanding a ten-year hiatus, horse-drawn street railway services continued in Halifax until April 1896 when the system, now operated by the [Halifax Electric Tramway Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia_Light_and_Power "Nova Scotia Light and Power"), completed the conversion to electric-powered operation. The street railway served Halifax until March 1949, when the war-worn trams were replaced by "trackless" electric trolley coaches.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-8)

The bright yellow trolleys, operated by utility company [Nova Scotia Light and Power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia_Light_and_Power "Nova Scotia Light and Power"), plied city streets exclusively until 1963, when they were supplemented by diesel buses for the first time. The system became all-diesel on January 1, 1970, the same day the City of Halifax took over operation under the name Halifax Transit.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-9) Some of Halifax's T-44 trolleybuses were sold to the [Toronto Transit Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Transit_Commission "Toronto Transit Commission") for parts for their [Western Flyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Flyer "New Flyer") E-700A.

Dartmouth Transit provided transit service in Dartmouth, a separate city at that time.

### Unification

[![Image 8: Old film photo of an older-model GM high-floor Metro Transit bus running southbound on Barrington Street next to the tall stone retaining wall of the Grand Parade. The bus is painted with a wide blue stripe down its length, the words Metro Transit in white at the rear of the bus. The photographer seems to be standing in front of the TD Building. Halifax City Hall is visible in the background.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Metro_Transit_Halifax_%2816579220042%29.jpg/250px-Metro_Transit_Halifax_%2816579220042%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Metro_Transit_Halifax_(16579220042).jpg)

Metro Transit bus on Barrington Street, 1990

Metro Transit, a single transit agency serving all of the greater Halifax-Dartmouth metropolitan area, began operations in March 1981.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-TransitHistory-3) The system was created by the Metropolitan Authority, an agency representing the former cities of Halifax and [Dartmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth,_Nova_Scotia "Dartmouth, Nova Scotia") as well as suburban Halifax County,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-10) to consolidate the transit operations of the Halifax Transit Corporation and Dartmouth Transit.

Metro Transit expanded in 1994 with the absorption of the [Dartmouth ferry services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax%E2%80%93Dartmouth_Ferry_Service "Halifax–Dartmouth Ferry Service") formerly operated by the city of Dartmouth. Ownership of the transit service was transferred to the newly created Halifax Regional Municipality when Halifax, Dartmouth, Bedford, and Halifax County were amalgamated in 1996. Since then, the service has been operated directly by the municipal government, and since October 2010 the agency has reported through the Transportation Standing Committee of [Halifax Regional Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax_Regional_Council "Halifax Regional Council"). The municipality announced on July 15, 2014 that it was changing the service's name to Halifax Transit to reflect the city's new brand.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-Halifax_Transit_brand_unveiled-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-12)

### MetroLink

The MetroLink service, a [bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") (BRT) express bus service, was developed in 2003 between the Halifax Regional Municipality, the [Province of Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia "Nova Scotia") and [Transport Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_Canada "Transport Canada")'s Urban Transportation Showcase Program, a five-year program designed to demonstrate and promote urban transportation strategies in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. The program selected cities across the country to showcase a number of different initiatives in reducing greenhouse gases. Halifax Regional Municipality's $13.3-million proposal for a BRT system was chosen, and $4.1 million was given by the [Government of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Canada "Government of Canada") toward this project. The remainder was funded by the Halifax Regional Municipality ($8.06 million), the Nova Scotia Department of Transportation and Public Works ($785,000) and the Nova Scotia Department of Energy ($80,000).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-13) Twenty [low floor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_floor "Low floor") buses were purchased from [New Flyer Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Flyer_Industries "New Flyer Industries") for the MetroLink service. These buses featured air conditioning, high-back reclining seats with footrests, carpeted walls, and ceilings to reduce road noise and vibration, a special livery and logo, and no advertisements both on the inside and outside. One of these buses, #600, was on public display on April 12, 2005, outside of City Hall. The bus was available for media and members of the general public to tour, and increase awareness of the new service.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-14)

The service was launched in phases, with the first phase on August 21, 2005. The first phase saw the construction of a new bus terminal in [Cole Harbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cole_Harbour,_Nova_Scotia "Cole Harbour, Nova Scotia") called Portland Hills Terminal, with a 230-space parking lot, including some spaces reserved for [carpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpool "Carpool") parking. Two routes were created at this time, the 159 Portland Hills Link and 165 Woodside Link.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-15)

The second phase was launched on February 20, 2006. This phase saw the construction of a new bus terminal in [Lower Sackville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Sackville,_Nova_Scotia "Lower Sackville, Nova Scotia") called the Sackville Terminal on Walker Ave, with a 315-space parking lot. One new route was created, the 185 Sackville Link.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-16)

#### Vehicles

In 2005, [Halifax Regional Municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax_Regional_Municipality "Halifax Regional Municipality") purchased twenty new buses from [New Flyer Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Flyer_Industries "New Flyer Industries") of [Winnipeg, Manitoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnipeg,_Manitoba "Winnipeg, Manitoba"). It was assumed at the time that HRM would purchase New Flyer's D40i Invero model, which New Flyer was marketing towards [BRT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") services, however HRM resisted and ordered 20 model D40LF instead, and were given fleet numbers 600 - 619. The D40LF was the current bus of choice at the time for Halifax Transit's regular fleet, so they opted to keep the status quo.

These twenty buses featured a new [livery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livery "Livery") on the outside, air conditioning on the inside (a first for Halifax Transit), bike racks, carpeting on the walls and ceiling to reduce road noise and vibrations, and larger plush high-back reclining chairs with arm and leg rests and custom designed fabric design. Also differentiating these buses from the rest of the Halifax Transit fleet are onboard transmitters for the [3M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3M "3M")[Opticom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opticom_System "Opticom System") system. Opticom is the system in place in HRM used by fire services and MetroLink, to allow emergency and transit vehicles to hold green lights and prevent them from turning red until the vehicle has passed through the intersection. The system was also used to trigger transit priority signals at certain intersections, allowing MetroLink buses to move into the intersection using special bus-only lanes before the rest of the vehicles can proceed. This allowed MetroLink buses at a red light to "jump" ahead of waiting cars.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-17)

#### Fares

Effective September 1, 2024,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-18) the MetroLink service had its own fare structure, separate from the rest of the Halifax Transit system. Cash fares cost an extra fifty cents over and above the regular fares. MetroLink had its own monthly bus pass, the MetroLink Pass, which could have been used on any Halifax Transit service. Passengers would have been able to use regular transit tickets or monthly bus passes (MetroPass), but they must deposit an additional fifty cents into the farebox.

| Category | Cash Fare | MetroLink Pass | With Transit Ticket, MetroPass, UPass or Transfer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Adult | $3.00 | $90.00 | +50 cents |
| Senior/Youth | $2.25 | $66.00 | +50 cents |
| Student | $3.00 | n/a | +50 cents |

#### Bus stops

Part of Halifax Regional Municipality's plans for distinguishing the MetroLink service from the rest of the Halifax Transit system involved creating special bus stop signs, bus shelters and info posts at MetroLink bus stops. The new bus stop signs featured the same colours and design as the livery on the buses, the new shelters featured the gold and blue MetroLink "swirl" along the back wall, and the new info posts, which displayed maps and schedule information for the three former MetroLink routes, they were also done in the same gold and blue swirl, with the stop name vertically oriented along the side.

#### Traffic changes

A number of changes were made to streets and intersections along the routes to help the MetroLink buses get ahead of the rest of traffic.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-19) The following changes were introduced:

*   Bus-only lanes and traffic priority signals along Portland Street in [Dartmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth,_Nova_Scotia "Dartmouth, Nova Scotia") for the route 159 and 165. The lanes and signals are located at the intersection of Portland Street and Woodlawn Road. The bus-only lanes allowed the MetroLink buses to bypass traffic waiting at a red light. Just before the light turns green, a special transit priority signal (a white vertical bar above the red stop light) comes on, allowing the bus to enter the intersection ahead of waiting vehicles.
*   Bus-only lanes and traffic priority signals along Windmill Road in the [Burnside Industrial Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnside_Industrial_Park "Burnside Industrial Park") for the route 185. The lanes and signals are located at the intersections of Windmill Road, Wright Ave and Akerley Blvd. They work in the same manner as described above.

#### Former planned development

Phase three of the MetroLink service was expected to take place within the next five years of the first three lines. This phase would have seen new terminals and MetroLink routes in other busy corridors such as [Clayton Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Park,_Nova_Scotia "Clayton Park, Nova Scotia") and [Spryfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spryfield,_Nova_Scotia "Spryfield, Nova Scotia").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-20)

Plans existed to introduce a new route to service the Cobequid Terminal, also in [Lower Sackville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Sackville,_Nova_Scotia "Lower Sackville, Nova Scotia") shortly after the 185 Sackville Link came into service. Destination signs on board the buses were even programmed with a route 184 Cobequid, and early maps of the MetroLink service showed a route 184 between Cobequid Terminal and [downtown Halifax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Halifax "Downtown Halifax"), however this plan seems to have been abandoned.

#### Impacts

*   The route 185 Sackville Line improved transit connections to downtown Halifax from Lower Sackville, since standard bus service on routes 87 & 1 takes 43 minutes in optimal conditions, and bus service on the route 80 (which travels via [Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedford,_Nova_Scotia "Bedford, Nova Scotia")) takes 1 hour 10 minutes.
*   Both routes 159 Portland Hills Link and 185 Sackville Link saw unprecedented ridership in the first few months of service. Initial rush hour schedules saw both routes running on 15-minute frequencies, however within months this was changed to 10-minutes. Also, both Portland Hills Terminal and the Sackville Terminal underwent expansions to their parking lots, bringing the combined capacity of both lots to 545 cars. Still, both parking lots were frequently full, with people parking on the driveways to the lots.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-21)

### Fuel leak

In 2014, a massive fuel leak spilling close to 200,000 litres of fuel at Halifax Transit's Burnside bus depot went undetected for almost four months.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-22) In addition to the cost of lost fuel, cleanup from local environmental damage and groundwater contamination as far as 1 km away cost Halifax Regional Municipality approximately $2.5 million.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-23) Before the discovery of the leak, Halifax Transit initially claimed that the excess fuel consumption was caused by higher usage during winter.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-24)

The municipal auditor general investigated the incident and recommended that Halifax Transit improve monitoring of fuel usage and inventory and improve training of employees involved in fuel handling.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-agfuel-25)

### System redesign

In January 2014, Halifax Regional Council approved a study to look at a major re-design of the city's transit system.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-26) The "Moving Forward Together Plan" (MFTP) was adopted in-principle by the council in April 2016. Proposed amendments to the plan were defeated in November 2016, with the exception of a change to the route of the Porters Lake MetroX and a short reprieve to attempt to increase ridership to save the #15 bus to York Redoubt.

The Moving Forward Together Plan is Halifax Transit's five-year improvement plan that outlines planned changes to the transit network from late 2016 to 2020. The plan aims to increase the proportion of resources dedicated to high-ridership routes, simplify the system and make it more understandable, improve service quality and reliability, and give priority to transit in the transportation network.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-movingforwardpage-27) The plan created a new classification system for bus routes, designating them as corridor, local, express, regional express, or rural routes. Corridor routes form the backbone of the revamped bus system, providing frequent service connecting transit terminals.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-MFTPplan-28)

Some critics called the plan inadequate, outlining various criticisms including inefficient and redundant route design, missing data and analysis, a long implementation period causing nuisance to riders, and a lack of network connectivity. In addition, critics characterised the "Moving Forward Together Plan" as disregarding the key principles that Halifax Transit identified through years of public engagement and consultation.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-29) Business groups have also noted both the current lack of service, and lack of proposed future service, along key corridors of the region.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-30)

The changes proposed under the Moving Forward Together Plan were implemented in stages each year, with the first round of changes taking place during the 2017/18 fiscal year. The final changes were delayed due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Nova_Scotia "COVID-19 pandemic in Nova Scotia") and chronic staffing shortages, but were ultimately completed during the 2024/25 fiscal year.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-31)

## Operations

### Bus services

There are 369 conventional buses in the fleet,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-202122businessplan-4) all of which are low floor and wheelchair accessible.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-metro2017-32)

Halifax Transit operates 63 conventional bus routes within the Urban Transit Service Boundary, broadly similar to the [metropolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area") region of [Halifax Regional Municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax_Regional_Municipality,_Nova_Scotia "Halifax Regional Municipality, Nova Scotia") ([Halifax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax,_Nova_Scotia_(former_city) "Halifax, Nova Scotia (former city)"), [Dartmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth,_Nova_Scotia "Dartmouth, Nova Scotia"), [Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedford,_Nova_Scotia "Bedford, Nova Scotia") and [Sackville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Sackville,_Nova_Scotia "Lower Sackville, Nova Scotia")), including the areas of [Eastern Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Passage,_Nova_Scotia "Eastern Passage, Nova Scotia"), [North Preston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Preston,_Nova_Scotia "North Preston, Nova Scotia")/[Cherry Brook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherry_Brook,_Nova_Scotia "Cherry Brook, Nova Scotia") and [Herring Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herring_Cove,_Nova_Scotia "Herring Cove, Nova Scotia"). Routes are numbered according to the region or type of service provided. The agency also operates three regional express routes and three rural routes.

The bus fleet is stored and maintained at two depots, namely the Burnside Transit Centre and the Ragged Lake Transit Centre.

#### Corridor routes

_Corridor routes_ are higher-ridership routes that provide frequent service for most of the day. They serve major destinations and transit terminals.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-MFTPplan-28) Following the round of service adjustments implemented in November 2021, there are ten corridor routes, numbered 1-10.

Corridor routes, considered the backbone of the bus system, operate at headways of 5–15 minutes during peak hours.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-MFTPplan-28)

#### Local routes

_Local routes_ provide connect neighbourhoods to corridor routes (at transit terminals).[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-MFTPplan-28) Local routes operate all day, except for four routes that operate at peak hours only: 26, 50, 57, and 93 (as well as parts of route 51).

#### Express routes

_Express routes_ provide limited-stop services to major destinations (e.g. downtown Halifax) at peak hours. Express bus stops are designated with a red route decal.

Express routes are sometimes paired with a local route, providing service along the local route before continuing along the express portion of the journey. For example, route 182 First Lake Express is an extended version of route 82 First Lake.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-MFTPplan-28)

This service type consolidated the former [MetroLink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MetroLink_(Halifax) "MetroLink (Halifax)") and "Urban Express" services.

#### Regional Express routes

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/MetroX_bus_at_Halifax_airport_2018.jpg/250px-MetroX_bus_at_Halifax_airport_2018.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MetroX_bus_at_Halifax_airport_2018.jpg)

A regional express bus (route 320) serving Halifax Stanfield International Airport

_Regional Express routes_ connect outlying areas to the regional centre. A higher fare is charged for these routes.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-MFTPplan-28)

Also branded as [MetroX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MetroX_(Halifax) "MetroX (Halifax)"), there are three Regional Express routes. These started operating in August 2009 and connect Tantallon, the Airport, and Porters Lake, respectively, to [Scotia Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotia_Square "Scotia Square") in downtown Halifax. The routes are handicap accessible and have facilities for bicycle carriage.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-33)

Among the three Regional Express routes, only route 320 (serving the airport) provides service on the weekend.

#### Rural routes

_Rural routes_ provide service to areas outside the Urban Transit Service Boundary which had transit service before the boundary was adopted.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-MFTPplan-28) There are three such routes, which connect rural areas to the nearest bus terminal.

### Ferry services

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/2022-08-15_01_Halifax_Transit_ferry%2C_VINCENT_COLEMAN_-_IMO_9850317_-_Canada.jpg/250px-2022-08-15_01_Halifax_Transit_ferry%2C_VINCENT_COLEMAN_-_IMO_9850317_-_Canada.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2022-08-15_01_Halifax_Transit_ferry,_VINCENT_COLEMAN_-_IMO_9850317_-_Canada.jpg)

Halifax Transit ferry, _Vincent Coleman_, arriving from Alderney Landing

Main article: [Halifax-Dartmouth Ferry Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax-Dartmouth_Ferry_Service "Halifax-Dartmouth Ferry Service")

Halifax Transit also provides two passenger ferry routes, one connecting [downtown Halifax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Halifax "Downtown Halifax") with [Alderney Landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alderney_Landing "Alderney Landing") in Dartmouth, and the other connecting with [Woodside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodside,_Nova_Scotia "Woodside, Nova Scotia"). Each route is serviced by a pair of vessels. The ferry services are integrated with the bus services; the fares are identical, and transfers are accepted between the two systems. The harbour ferries boarded approximately 1.7 million passengers in the 2024/25 fiscal year.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-202425report-2) Each ferry carries up to 398 passengers. All routes are handicap accessible and have provision to carry bicycles.

The agency operates a fleet of five ferries built in the 2010s by [A. F. Theriault Shipyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._F._Theriault_Shipyard "A. F. Theriault Shipyard"). As of 2023, a third ferry route – connecting downtown Halifax and Bedford – is in planning.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-34)

### Access-A-Bus

Halifax Transit also provides Access-A-Bus, a dial-a-ride paratransit service for people who cannot use the conventional transit service due to physical or cognitive disability.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-accessabus-35) This was created in 1981, the same year Metro Transit was formed.

In the 2024/25 financial year, the Access-A-Bus service had approximately 171,000 boardings.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-202425report-2)

### Fares and passes

Halifax Transit has four main fare categories: Adult (18 years & up), Senior (65+ years), Child (13 – 17 years), and Student (for full-time students with valid student photo ID card). Anyone with a ticket, pass or transfer for the regular service can pay the difference in cash fare to use the more expensive Regional Express (MetroX) service. Monthly passes allow for unlimited use of ferries and buses, and are sold through various channels including municipal service centres, drug stores, some supermarkets, and the convenience store at the Bridge Terminal.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-passes-36)

Digital tickets and passes can be purchased using HFXGO, the agency's free mobile fare payment app. Launched on November 2, 2023, the app is available for Android and iOS devices.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-37) Initially, digital tickets or passes had to be shown to the bus driver or ferry terminal attendant upon boarding.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-38) Fare validation machines have since been installed at ferry terminals and on buses.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-39)

A Canadian National Institute for the Blind (CNIB) identification card can be used to obtain free travel on Halifax Transit's buses and ferries. A university student bus pass (called U-pass) is available to students of [Saint Mary's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Mary's_University_(Halifax) "Saint Mary's University (Halifax)"), [Mount Saint Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Saint_Vincent_University "Mount Saint Vincent University"), [King's College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_King's_College "University of King's College"), [Dalhousie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalhousie_University "Dalhousie University"), [Nova Scotia Community College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia_Community_College "Nova Scotia Community College") (Halifax campuses) and [Nova Scotia College of Art and Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia_College_of_Art_and_Design_University "Nova Scotia College of Art and Design University"). The cost is included in tuition fees. Halifax Transit offers a low-income bus pass sold for 50 per cent of the regular price to eligible applicants.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-lowincomeprogram-40)

In 2021, Halifax Transit launched a pilot program to provide high school students with free transit passes. The program aims to provide youth with convenient transportation and encourage the use of public transit. The program is currently being piloted at all schools in the [HRCE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax_Regional_Centre_for_Education "Halifax Regional Centre for Education"), and CSAP schools in the Halifax Regional Municipality, as well as for home-schooled students in the region, namely [Dartmouth High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth_High_School_(Nova_Scotia) "Dartmouth High School (Nova Scotia)"), [École Mosaïque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_Mosa%C3%AFque?action=edit&redlink=1 "École Mosaïque (page does not exist)"), [École du Sommet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_du_Sommet "École du Sommet"), and [Prince Andrew High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Andrew_High_School "Prince Andrew High School").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-41) In November 2022, council voted to expand the program to four Dartmouth junior high schools.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-signalnov2022-42)

Transfers are issued upon request on all Halifax Transit buses and ferries. A transfer allows the user to transfer between multiple conventional route buses and ferries travelling in any direction without having to pay an additional fare. A transfer also allows users to transfer to [MetroX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MetroX_(Halifax) "MetroX (Halifax)") buses at a reduced fare. Transfers are valid for 90 minutes after the last scheduled stop on the current run of the route where it was issued. Holders of a valid XPass (the monthly pass for the MetroX) do not require transfers.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-43)

### Schedules and route information

Route information can be accessed through the Halifax Transit Departures number, (902) 480-8000. Individual route schedules are available on Halifax Transit's website. Most terminals have screens that display anticipated arrival times of buses that service the terminal.

### Departures

In early 2016, Halifax Transit released their next-generation AVL-based system called Departures. The system was first launched on May 15, 2016, with the introduction of the Departures Line, and as of July 2016 the rollout of the updated Departures Board that replaces the older GoTime departure displays found at terminals across the system. The Departures Board works similar to the previous GoTime-based departures display, with the exception that instead of showing the next two bus arrival times, will display the bay number and the next bus departure time, either showing the next hour and minute or the number of minutes before the bus departs, or "delayed" if the bus is behind by a certain number of minutes. It will also only show buses set to arrive in the next while, versus the older display which would show "(not scheduled)" for any route not running at that point in time.

The Departures Line works similarly to the previous GoTime IVR (Interactive Voice Response) system. Instead of dialing "(902) 480-" plus the four-digit number found on bus stop signage, one dials (902) 480-8000 and following the voice responses, one would input the bus stop number to access route departure times. The system gives the estimated departure time if available, scheduled times if the bus is not reporting real-time data or is delayed by a number of minutes, adjusted time to depart when schedule adjustments are made, and will announce when a bus is arriving within the minute.

### Accessibility

On December 16, 2016 Halifax Transit began piloting an automated stop announcement system on several bus routes, providing both auditory and visual notice of approaching bus stops, as well as announcing the route of each bus on arrival at a bus stop.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-44) By January 30, 2017, all conventional buses provided the automated stop announcement.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-45) As of June 8, 2017, all conventional buses in the Halifax Transit fleet were low floor and accessible to wheelchairs.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-metro2017-32)

Although Halifax Transit's vehicle fleet is considered accessible, many of the bus stops are not. At some stops, the lack of an appropriate landing area prevents the deployment of a bus [wheelchair ramp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheelchair_ramp "Wheelchair ramp"). Other stops lack sidewalk connections. Halifax Transit is upgrading bus stops and aims to make all stops accessible by 2030.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-46)

*   Regional Express routes (numbered 300-399)

## Rapid Transit Network

In May 2020, Halifax Transit presented a plan to regional council to implement a new Rapid Transit Strategy. The strategy proposes the creation of a new Rapid Transit Network comprising four new bus rapid transit (BRT) lines and three new ferry routes. The estimated capital cost is around C$300–325 million, while operational costs are estimated at $15–22 million.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-47) Halifax Regional Council unanimously endorsed the plan on May 26, 2020.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-endorsecbc-48)

As of 2021, Halifax is seeking funding for the project from other levels of government.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-abmmarch2021-49) Funding for the planning and design of one of the proposed ferry routes, the Halifax-Mill Cove (Bedford) service, was announced in June 2021. Halifax Transit originally planned to launch the service in 2024.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halifax_Transit&printable=yes#cite_note-50)[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]

## In popular culture

**Answer**

The bus that travels onto Oxford Street and terminates at the terminal right by the Walmart and Sobeys is **Route 24 – “Leiblin Park”**.

| Feature | Route 24 |
|---------|----------|
| **Where it goes** | The outbound leg of Route 24 turns onto **Oxford Street** (see the route description). |
| **Where it ends** | The route terminates at **Mumford Terminal Bay 1/2**. The terminal is part of the Halifax Shopping Centre complex, which is anchored by a **Walmart** and a **Sobeys** (street‑side stores), according to the shopping‑centre page. |
| **Why it fits the description** | It follows the specified street (Oxford) and ends at the terminal that sits between the two mentioned retail anchors. |

**Sources**

1. **Halifax Transit – Route descriptions** – shows the outbound leg of Route 24 includes “right on Oxford Street” and ends at “Mumford Terminal Bay 1/2.”  
   *Source: [Halifax Transit Route Descriptions](https://www.halifax.ca/transportation/halifax-transit/routes-schedules/route-descriptions) – Route 24 section.*  

2. **Halifax Shopping Centre – Wikipedia** – lists the mall’s anchors as **Sobeys** and **Walmart** and notes that the mall’s hub is the **Mumford Terminal**.  
   *Source: [Halifax Shopping Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax_Shopping_Centre) – “Mumford Terminal … Affiliate anchors: Sobeys and Walmart.”*  

3. **Halifax Transit – Route 24 PDF (schedule & stops)** – confirms that one of the terminal stops is “Mumford Terminal Bay 1” (the destination), reinforcing that the terminal is the same one by the retail anchors.  
   *Source: [Route 24 PDF](https://www.halifax.ca/sites/default/files/documents/transportation/halifax-transit/route24_feb23.pdf).*
